title: He lost his sight in Class 8, reading a paragraph aloud. He cracked UPSC anyway. October 7, 2026.
excerpt: From a ghazal singer honored decades into her career, to a surgeon operating across continents, to a metro line expanding without fanfare, October 7's five stories are about work that outlasts the moment it was made in.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about something that had to be sustained to matter - a musical form perfected over a lifetime, a surgical technique trusted across 10,000 kilometres, a community-music practice kept going for 15 years, a metro corridor built one station at a time, and a UPSC preparation rebuilt after a first failure. None of it happened in a single moment.

October 7, 1914: she was born in a small town in Uttar Pradesh. The world would later call her the Queen of Ghazals

Begum Akhtar was born in Faizabad on October 7, 1914, and became one of Hindustani classical music's greatest voices in ghazal, dadra and thumri. She received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award in 1972 and the Padma Shri, before being posthumously conferred the Padma Bhushan.

He operated on a patient 10,000 km away. The round trip took under 150 milliseconds

Dr. Mohit Bhandari performed the world's longest-distance robotic telesurgery on May 2, 2026, remotely operating on a patient in Indore while in Perth, Australia, using the SSI Mantra system - completing the procedure in about three minutes with latency low enough to trust a scalpel to.

He plays violin for the LA Philharmonic. He also plays it inside homeless shelters and jails

Vijay Gupta joined the LA Philharmonic in 2007 at age 19, then founded Street Symphony in 2011 - bringing live classical music directly into LA's homeless shelters, clinics, jails and state hospitals. The work later earned him a 2018 MacArthur Fellowship.

A Tier-2 city just expanded its metro network - no fanfare, just 11 new stations

Indore inaugurated Priority Corridor-2 of its metro on September 6, 2026, an 11 km, 11-station expansion costing roughly Rs 2,850 crore, pushing the city's total network to about 17 km across 16 stations - modern urban rail reaching beyond India's traditional metro capitals.

He lost his sight in Class 8, reading a paragraph aloud. His father left soon after. He never learned Braille - he cracked UPSC anyway

Manu Garg was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa in Class 8 and lost his sight entirely. Raised by his mother alone, he relied on screen readers and audiobooks through Delhi University and JNU, failed the UPSC mains in 2023, and returned in 2024 to secure All India Rank 91.

Five stories, one thread: a singer honored across decades, a surgeon trusted across continents, a musician who kept showing up for 15 years, a city that built its metro one corridor at a time, and a student who came back after failing once. All of it took longer than a headline.
